title: Introduction to LLM serving with SGLang - Philip Kiely and Yineng Zhang, Baseten
talk_summary: A hands-on workshop introducing SGLang as an open-source LLM serving framework, covering basic deployment, CUDA graph batch-size tuning, and Eagle 3 speculative decoding parameter sweeps.

takeaways.technique: Sweep configs against a representative workload, not defaults
takeaways.what_they_do: They run a script that enumerates combinations of speculative-decoding parameters (steps, top-k, draft tokens) across batch sizes and pick the best by measured speed and acceptance rate, explicitly warning that benchmark prompts must match production traffic.
takeaways.evidence_quote: be sure to set the prompts to things that are representative of your actual workload

takeaways.technique: Observe runtime logs to detect when an optimization silently turns off
takeaways.what_they_do: They watch server logs during a benchmark and notice a fast-path (CUDA graph) is disabled because the live batch exceeded the configured max, then raise the limit to cover realistic load.
takeaways.evidence_quote: during the decoding the CUDA graph is disabled and we actually we want to enable CUDA graph
takeaways.numbers: CUDA graph max batch size default 8 on L4; raised to 32 to cover ~10-13 concurrent requests

takeaways.technique: Match serving config to realistic concurrency
takeaways.what_they_do: They size the batch/graph limit to the actual concurrent request count seen in benchmarks rather than leaving a conservative default that disables the optimization under load.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we can handle the realistic batch during benchmark

takeaways.technique: Pick runtime per model by compatibility vs performance
takeaways.what_they_do: Baseten runs multiple runtimes (SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) and chooses per model, using vLLM mainly for broad compatibility and others for performance.
takeaways.evidence_quote: where we use VLM is oftentimes for compatibility
